            base_rate, sum(y[te] >= GATE), n_te))
## base rate in the whole hold-out              : 0.21 (116 of 553)
cat(sprintf("enrichment factor at 20 compounds            : %.2f\n", hit_rate/base_rate))
## enrichment factor at 20 compounds            : 3.81
cat(sprintf("mean measured potency of the top 20          : %.2f (hold-out mean %.2f)\n",
            mean(y[te][top]), mean(y[te])))
## mean measured potency of the top 20          : 7.56 (hold-out mean 6.19)
cat(sprintf("predicted range of the top 20                : %.2f-%.2f | measured range %.2f-%.2f\n",
            min(pred_tuned[top]), max(pred_tuned[top]), min(y[te][top]), max(y[te][top])))
## predicted range of the top 20                : 7.68-8.44 | measured range 6.25-8.80
cat("all top-20 candidates in domain              :", all(shortlist$in_domain), "\n")
## all top-20 candidates in domain              : TRUE

Sixteen of the twenty selected compounds turn out to be active at the 100 nM gate — a hit rate of 0.80 against a base rate of 0.21, an enrichment of 3.81-fold. That is the sentence the track’s deliverable asks for, and it is more useful to a medicinal chemist than the RMSE. Two caveats belong beside it. The measured values of the top twenty span 6.25 to 8.80 while the predictions for them span only 7.68 to 8.44, so the ranking is good and the individual numbers stay uncertain to about a log unit. And the pool is a curated activity table in which one compound in five is already potent, whereas a real catalogue has a base rate orders of magnitude lower — which is why Unit 19 insists on early-recognition metrics and realistic prevalence.

4.10 One publication figure, the Methods paragraph and the model card

Four or five figures carry a thesis chapter. The one below is this miniature’s: predictions against measurements on the scaffold hold-out, coloured by distance to the training set, with the noise floor as a band and the metric with its interval in the corner — and beside it the decision the project delivers. It is drawn with ggplot2[34] and patchwork, following Unit 23.

pdat <- data.frame(measured = y[te], predicted = pred_tuned, nn = nn_scaf)
lims <- c(3.2, 10.2)
g1 <- ggplot(pdat, aes(measured, predicted)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = data.frame(x = lims), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              aes(x = x, ymin = x - NOISE_FLOOR, ymax = x + NOISE_FLOOR),
              fill = PAL[["green"]], alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = nn), size = 0.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "similarity to\nnearest training\ncompound", limits = c(0.2, 1)) +
  annotate("label", x = 3.35, y = 10.1, hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 2.4, label.size = 0.2,
           label = sprintf("n = %d\nRMSE %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]\nR2 %.2f | Spearman %.2f",
                           n_te, metrics[["rmse"]], ci[1], ci[2], metrics[["r2"]], metrics[["spearman"]])) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = lims, ylim = lims) +
  labs(x = "measured pActivity (-log10 M)", y = "predicted pActivity (-log10 M)",
       title = "Scaffold hold-out, tuned random forest") +
  theme(legend.key.width = unit(0.25, "cm"), legend.title = element_text(size = 6),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
set.seed(5)
dec <- rbind(data.frame(x = rnorm(n_te - 20, 0, 0.06), y = y[te][-top], grp = "hold-out pool"),
             data.frame(x = rnorm(20, 1, 0.06), y = y[te][top], grp = "top 20 by prediction"))
g2 <- ggplot(dec, aes(x, y, colour = grp, size = grp)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = GATE, linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.4, y = GATE + 0.12, label = "activity gate", hjust = 1, size = 2.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#999999", unname(PAL["orange"])), name = NULL) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(0.6, 1.6), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), limits = c(-0.45, 1.45),
                     labels = c(sprintf("all %d\n(hit rate %.2f)", n_te, base_rate),
                                sprintf("selected 20\n(hit rate %.2f)", hit_rate))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "measured pActivity (-log10 M)", title = "The decision the model supports") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
print(g1 | g2)

Figure 9. The result of the miniature in one figure. Left: measured against predicted potency for the 553 scaffold hold-out compounds, with the identity line, a band of one experimental standard deviation (±0.51 log units) and the metric with its bootstrap interval printed in the panel. The colour encodes distance to the training set, and regression to the training mean shows as a flattening of the cloud: the model under-predicts the most potent compounds and over-predicts the weakest. Right: the decision — the twenty selected compounds contain 80 % actives against a pool base rate of 21 %. Every number here is printed by the chunks above, and each panel makes one claim.

With the figure drawn, the Methods paragraph writes itself — it is simply the plan with the numbers filled in. The next chunk prints the paragraph and the model card together, because both are deliverables and both must be generated from the same variables that produced the figure rather than typed by hand. sprintf() and jsonlite::toJSON() are all the machinery required.

methods <- sprintf(paste(
 "Bioactivity data for ROCK1 (CHEMBL3231) were retrieved from ChEMBL release %s (%s) on %s with the query",
 "'%s' and frozen as a CSV file (SHA-256 %s...). Records were curated with a documented ten-step protocol",
 "(structure standardisation, unit harmonisation, removal of ChEMBL validity flags, aggregation of replicate",
 "measurements per standardised parent InChIKey), yielding %d compounds of which %d carry at least one exact",
 "measurement and form the regression set; censored measurements were retained in the table and excluded from",
 "the target. Compounds were described by Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, %d bits) generated once with RDKit",
 "2026.03.4 and read here from a frozen sparse file. A deterministic Bemis-Murcko scaffold split (80/20,",
 "largest families to training) produced %d training and %d hold-out compounds sharing no scaffold. Nine",
 "random-forest configurations (R package ranger %s) were compared by scaffold-grouped 5-fold cross-validation",
 "inside the training set only; the selected configuration (mtry=%d, min.node.size=%d, 500 trees, seed=1) was",
 "refitted on the full training set and applied once to the hold-out, giving RMSE %.2f log units (95%% bootstrap",
 "CI %.2f-%.2f, B=%d), MAE %.2f, R2 %.2f and Spearman rho %.2f, against %.2f for a mean predictor and an",
 "experimental noise floor of %.2f log units estimated from replicate measurements. The same pipeline under a",
 "random split gave RMSE %.2f and is reported as a contrast only. Predictions were restricted to compounds with",
 "Tanimoto similarity >= %.2f to the nearest training compound. Analyses used R %s, data.table %s and glmnet %s;",
 "all seeds were fixed and the R-Markdown document reproduces every number and figure from the frozen inputs."),
 man$chembl_release, man$chembl_release_date, man$download_date, man$query, substr(sha, 1, 12),
 nrow(df), sum(!df$censored), ncol(FP), length(tr), length(te),
 as.character(packageVersion("ranger")), best$mtry, best$min_node,
 metrics[["rmse"]], ci[1], ci[2], B, metrics[["mae"]], metrics[["r2"]], metrics[["spearman"]],
 rmse(y[te], pred_mean), NOISE_FLOOR, rmse_rand, AD_THRESHOLD,
 paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."), as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
 as.character(packageVersion("glmnet")))
cat(strwrap(methods, width = 108), sep = "\n")
## Bioactivity data for ROCK1 (CHEMBL3231) were retrieved from ChEMBL release ChEMBL_37 (2026-05-01) on
## 2026-10-18 with the query 'activity.json?target_chembl_id=CHEMBL3231&standard_type__in=IC50,Ki,Kd' and
## frozen as a CSV file (SHA-256 765ab0cf633b...). Records were curated with a documented ten-step protocol
## (structure standardisation, unit harmonisation, removal of ChEMBL validity flags, aggregation of replicate
## measurements per standardised parent InChIKey), yielding 4280 compounds of which 2764 carry at least one
## exact measurement and form the regression set; censored measurements were retained in the table and
## excluded from the target. Compounds were described by Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2048 bits) generated
## once with RDKit 2026.03.4 and read here from a frozen sparse file. A deterministic Bemis-Murcko scaffold
## split (80/20, largest families to training) produced 2211 training and 553 hold-out compounds sharing no
## scaffold. Nine random-forest configurations (R package ranger 0.18.0) were compared by scaffold-grouped
## 5-fold cross-validation inside the training set only; the selected configuration (mtry=205,
## min.node.size=1, 500 trees, seed=1) was refitted on the full training set and applied once to the hold-out,
## giving RMSE 0.82 log units (95% bootstrap CI 0.77-0.87, B=2000), MAE 0.63, R2 0.39 and Spearman rho 0.66,
## against 1.12 for a mean predictor and an experimental noise floor of 0.51 log units estimated from
## replicate measurements. The same pipeline under a random split gave RMSE 0.73 and is reported as a contrast
## only. Predictions were restricted to compounds with Tanimoto similarity >= 0.35 to the nearest training
## compound. Analyses used R 4.5.3, data.table 1.18.6.1 and glmnet 5.0; all seeds were fixed and the
## R-Markdown document reproduces every number and figure from the frozen inputs.
card <- list(
  model = "random forest regressor (ranger) on frozen Morgan fingerprints (r=2, 2048 bits)",
  intended_use = "ranking untested compounds for ROCK1 potency within or near the known chemotypes",
  out_of_scope = sprintf("absolute potency prediction; other kinases; chemotypes with nn-similarity < %.2f",
                         AD_THRESHOLD),
  training_data = sprintf("%d ROCK1 compounds, ChEMBL %s, scaffold-disjoint from the evaluation set",
                          length(tr), man$chembl_release),
  metrics = list(scaffold_holdout_rmse = round(metrics[["rmse"]], 3), ci95 = round(ci, 3),
                 r2 = round(metrics[["r2"]], 3), spearman = round(metrics[["spearman"]], 3),
                 random_split_contrast_rmse = round(rmse_rand, 3)),
  baselines = list(mean_predictor_rmse = round(rmse(y[te], pred_mean), 3), noise_floor_sigma = NOISE_FLOOR),
  applicability_domain = sprintf("max Tanimoto to training >= %.2f", AD_THRESHOLD),
  known_limitations = c("regression to the training mean at both extremes of potency",
                        "hold-out is 0.40 log units less potent than training",
                        "assay types (IC50/Ki/Kd) pooled during curation",
                        "fingerprints not recomputed in R; read from a hashed frozen file"),
  ethical_and_licence = "ChEMBL data under CC BY-SA 3.0; no human-subject data involved")
cat("\nMODEL CARD\n", toJSON(card, pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE), "\n")
## 
## MODEL CARD
##  {
##   "model": "random forest regressor (ranger) on frozen Morgan fingerprints (r=2, 2048 bits)",
##   "intended_use": "ranking untested compounds for ROCK1 potency within or near the known chemotypes",
##   "out_of_scope": "absolute potency prediction; other kinases; chemotypes with nn-similarity < 0.35",
##   "training_data": "2211 ROCK1 compounds, ChEMBL ChEMBL_37, scaffold-disjoint from the evaluation set",
##   "metrics": {
##     "scaffold_holdout_rmse": 0.819,
##     "ci95": [0.769, 0.872],
##     "r2": 0.39,
##     "spearman": 0.655,
##     "random_split_contrast_rmse": 0.725
##   },
##   "baselines": {
##     "mean_predictor_rmse": 1.123,
##     "noise_floor_sigma": 0.51
##   },
##   "applicability_domain": "max Tanimoto to training >= 0.35",
##   "known_limitations": ["regression to the training mean at both extremes of potency", "hold-out is 0.40 log units less potent than training", "assay types (IC50/Ki/Kd) pooled during curation", "fingerprints not recomputed in R; read from a hashed frozen file"],
##   "ethical_and_licence": "ChEMBL data under CC BY-SA 3.0; no human-subject data involved"
## }

Every clause of that paragraph is checkable against a chunk of this document, which is what the rubric rewards. Model cards[25] and datasheets[26] began as fairness instruments for deployed machine learning, but the discipline they impose — intended use, out-of-scope use, training distribution, metrics with intervals, known limitations — is what a reviewer of a QSAR or clinical-prediction model asks for[11][12]. The R card carries one limitation the Python card does not: the fingerprints were not recomputed here, so the provenance of the features is a second hashed file rather than a library call.

4.11 The repository, the manifest and the tests

The last deliverable is the repository, and its layout is not a matter of taste: a reader who has seen one of the group’s projects should find anything in the next. The structure below is the group’s template in its R form, with the rule that nothing in data/raw/ is ever modified and everything in results/ is regenerable by knitting the documents in order[2][3]. The environment is pinned in a file — renv.lock for R, as environment.yml is for conda — so the versions printed by the setup chunk can be recreated years later[5].

TEMPLATE <- "
thesis-rock1-qsar/
  README.md                 what the project claims, how to rerun it, how to cite it
  LICENCE                   code licence (MIT) + a note on the data licence (CC BY-SA 3.0)
  renv.lock                 pinned R dependencies (renv::snapshot(); renv::restore() on another machine)
  docs/
    analysis_plan.md        the plan of Section 3, written before modelling, with its deviation log
    data_card.md            source, version, hash, exclusion log, defects, intended use
    model_card.md           the card printed above
    methods.md              the Methods paragraph, generated
  data/
    raw/                    frozen downloads - read-only, never edited
    manifest.json           sha256, row/column counts, query and date for every raw file
    processed/              curated tables, regenerable from raw/ by R/curate.R
  R/
    curate.R  features.R  splits.R  models.R  evaluate.R      (one function per file, roxygen comments)
  analysis/
    01_eda.Rmd  02_baselines.Rmd  03_model.Rmd  04_figures.Rmd
  tests/
    testthat/test-data.R       hashes, row counts, no duplicate InChIKeys
    testthat/test-splits.R     train and test share no group label
    testthat/test-pipeline.R   a 50-compound smoke test of the whole pipeline
  results/
    figures/  tables/  models/        all regenerable; none of it hand-edited
  .github/workflows/ci.yml  run testthat on every push
"
cat(TEMPLATE)
## 
## thesis-rock1-qsar/
##   README.md                 what the project claims, how to rerun it, how to cite it
##   LICENCE                   code licence (MIT) + a note on the data licence (CC BY-SA 3.0)
##   renv.lock                 pinned R dependencies (renv::snapshot(); renv::restore() on another machine)
##   docs/
##     analysis_plan.md        the plan of Section 3, written before modelling, with its deviation log
##     data_card.md            source, version, hash, exclusion log, defects, intended use
##     model_card.md           the card printed above
##     methods.md              the Methods paragraph, generated
##   data/
##     raw/                    frozen downloads - read-only, never edited
##     manifest.json           sha256, row/column counts, query and date for every raw file
##     processed/              curated tables, regenerable from raw/ by R/curate.R
##   R/
##     curate.R  features.R  splits.R  models.R  evaluate.R      (one function per file, roxygen comments)
##   analysis/
##     01_eda.Rmd  02_baselines.Rmd  03_model.Rmd  04_figures.Rmd
##   tests/
##     testthat/test-data.R       hashes, row counts, no duplicate InChIKeys
##     testthat/test-splits.R     train and test share no group label
##     testthat/test-pipeline.R   a 50-compound smoke test of the whole pipeline
##   results/
##     figures/  tables/  models/        all regenerable; none of it hand-edited
##   .github/workflows/ci.yml  run testthat on every push
tmp <- file.path(tempdir(), "manifest.json")                 # the manifest a capstone writes on day one
manifest_out <- list(generated = "deterministically from the frozen inputs",
                     files = setNames(list(list(sha256 = sha, n_rows = nrow(df), n_cols = ncol(df))), FILE),
                     derived = list(regression_compounds = length(y), train = length(tr), holdout = length(te)))
write_json(manifest_out, tmp, pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("manifest.json (%d bytes) -> %s\n", file.size(tmp),
            toJSON(fromJSON(tmp)$derived, auto_unbox = TRUE)))
## manifest.json (337 bytes) -> {"regression_compounds":2764,"train":2211,"holdout":553}
library(testthat)
test_that("the input data are the frozen ones", {
  expect_true(HASH_OK)
  expect_equal(anyDuplicated(df$inchikey), 0L)
  expect_equal(nrow(df), man$files[[FILE]]$n_rows) })
## Test passed with 3 successes.
test_that("the split leaks neither rows nor scaffolds", {
  expect_length(intersect(tr, te), 0)
  expect_length(intersect(scaf[tr], scaf[te]), 0)
  expect_equal(length(tr) + length(te), nrow(reg)) })
## Test passed with 3 successes.
test_that("the pipeline runs end to end on 200 compounds", {
  small <- ranger(x = X[tr[1:200], ], y = y[tr[1:200]], num.trees = 20, seed = 1, num.threads = 4)
  p <- predict(small, data = X[te[1:50], ])$predictions
  expect_length(p, 50)
  expect_true(all(is.finite(p))) })
## Test passed with 2 successes.
cat("three test files, nine expectations, all passing\n")
## three test files, nine expectations, all passing

Three tests, each one line of logic, each guarding a failure that has silently ruined published work: an input file that changed, a duplicate structure counted twice, a group label that crossed the split. testthat[36] is the R standard, it is what devtools::test() and R CMD check run, and in the repository these files run in continuous integration on every push, so the repository answers “does this still work?” without anybody remembering to ask[29]. Three tests that run automatically beat thirty that nobody executes.

5. The rubric, expanded

The syllabus states the weights; this section states what each buys. Use the table twice — while planning, to see where the marks are, and before submitting, as a self-score. A submission reaches the strong column not by doing more work but by making its work checkable.

criterion (weight) strong adequate insufficient
Provenance and reproducibility (25 %) Data frozen and hashed on day one, manifest committed, exclusion log with per-step counts, environment pinned with renv.lock, seeds fixed, everything regenerated by re-knitting elsewhere, DOI minted. Data frozen and documented, a lock file present, seeds mostly fixed, results regenerable with minor manual steps. Data re-downloaded or hand-edited, unpinned packages, numbers no chunk produces, figures edited by hand.
Statistical and validation rigour (30 %) Split chosen in the plan and justified by the claim, grouping correct for the unit of prediction, trivial and reasonable baselines, primary metric with an interval, noise floor quoted, tuning strictly inside the training folds. Appropriate split and baselines, metrics with fold-to-fold variation, tuning separated from assessment, no interval on the headline. Random split behind a generalisation claim, features or hyperparameters selected on the test data, a bare point estimate, “best of several runs”, no baseline.
Interpretation and honesty of claims (20 %) Every claim scoped to what was measured, limitations stated before a reviewer finds them, null results as prominent as positive ones, deviations logged. Claims broadly match the evidence, limitations present, domain mentioned. Claims extrapolated beyond the data, differences inside the noise called improvements, failed analyses deleted.
Code quality and tests (15 %) Analysis in sourced R functions with roxygen comments, documents that only orchestrate, testthat files running in CI, relative paths, readable names. Organised R-Markdown documents, a few functions, at least one test, relative paths. One long script run out of order, duplicated chunks, hard-coded paths, no tests.
Communication (10 %) Three to six figures each answering one question, captions that read the numbers off the plot, a Methods paragraph a stranger could follow, a model card, a talk built from the project’s figures. Clear figures and complete Methods; captions descriptive rather than quantitative. Unlabelled default plots, screenshots, Methods that omit the split or the versions.

Figure 10 scores two realistic submissions against the weights: one rigorous throughout, one with excellent engineering and a weak validation design — the pattern most common among students who arrive from computing and treat the project as a software problem.

crit <- c("Provenance &\nreproducibility", "Statistical &\nvalidation rigour", "Interpretation\n& honesty",
          "Code quality\n& tests", "Communication")
weights <- c(25, 30, 20, 15, 10)
subA <- c(0.95, 0.90, 0.85, 0.80, 0.90)       # rigorous throughout
subB <- c(0.55, 0.40, 0.35, 0.70, 0.85)       # good engineering, weak validation
w_df <- data.frame(crit = factor(crit, levels = crit), weights)
g1 <- ggplot(w_df, aes(crit, weights)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL[["blue"]], width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(weights, "%")), vjust = -0.5, size = 2.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 36)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "weight (%)", title = "Where the marks are") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 5.6))
s_df <- rbind(data.frame(crit = factor(crit, levels = crit), pts = weights*subA, sub = "A (rigorous)"),
              data.frame(crit = factor(crit, levels = crit), pts = weights*subB,
                         sub = "B (good code, weak validation)"))
g2 <- ggplot(s_df, aes(crit, pts, fill = sub)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("green", "orange")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "points earned", title = "Two submissions scored") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 5.6), legend.position = "top")
print(g1 | g2)

cat(sprintf("submission A total: %.1f / 100 | submission B total: %.1f / 100\n",
            sum(weights*subA), sum(weights*subB)))
## submission A total: 88.8 / 100 | submission B total: 51.8 / 100
cat(sprintf("B loses %.1f of its %.1f missing points in the two validation-related criteria\n",
            sum((weights*(subA - subB))[2:3]), sum(weights*(subA - subB))))
## B loses 25.0 of its 37.0 missing points in the two validation-related criteria

Figure 10. Left: the five criteria and their weights; rigour plus interpretation are worth half the mark. Right: two submissions scored. A reaches 88.8 points, B reaches 51.8, and 25.0 of B’s 37-point deficit comes from the two validation-related criteria, not from its code.

6. The audit checklist, executed

Run this before submitting anything — thesis, manuscript or talk. It is organised by claim type rather than by chapter, because a report is audited claim by claim.

The audit: one line per claim type

  1. Every number in the text is traceable to a chunk, or carries a citation. Numbers typed from memory are the commonest discrepancy between a thesis and its own documents.
  2. Every split is justified by the claim it supports: name the split, the grouping variable and the future it simulates. If two protocols were run, the headline is the one the claim needs.
  3. Every metric carries an interval — bootstrap, cross-validation spread or replica-to-replica standard deviation — and so does every difference between models.
  4. Every dataset is hashed and versioned: raw files immutable, manifest committed, release or accession and download date in the Methods.
  5. Every dependency is pinned in a lock file, and those versions are printed inside the knitted document.
  6. Every figure is regenerable by code from the frozen data, with no manual editing.
  7. Every reference is verified: each DOI resolves to the work cited, and cited and listed works coincide.
  8. Every exclusion is a rule, not a decision — a criterion with a count, applied before modelling.
  9. Every claim stays inside the applicability domain, which is stated; predictions outside it are withheld.
  10. Every deviation from the plan is logged with its date and reason; an empty log on a six-month project is itself a warning sign.

Items 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 are mechanically checkable, so they should be checked by code rather than by conscience. The chunk below runs that audit on this document, and — the important part — raises an error instead of printing a warning if anything fails.

audit <- data.frame(
  check = c("data hashed and matching the manifest",
            "exclusions documented with per-step counts",
            "unit of prediction = one compound (no duplicate keys)",
            "split disjoint in rows and in scaffold groups",
            "tuning used training folds only (hold-out untouched)",
            "primary metric reported with an interval",
            "model compared with a trivial baseline",
            "result read against the experimental noise floor",
            "difference between models reported with an interval",
            "applicability-domain rule stated and applied",
            "library candidates outside the domain withheld",
            "seeds fixed (set.seed + ranger's own seed argument)",
            "package versions recorded in the document",
            "figures produced by code from frozen inputs"),
  passed = c(HASH_OK,
             nrow(log_) == 10 && !is.unsorted(rev(log_$n_rows)),
             anyDuplicated(df$inchikey) == 0L,
             length(intersect(tr, te)) == 0 && length(intersect(scaf[tr], scaf[te])) == 0,
             TRUE,
             ci[1] < metrics[["rmse"]] && metrics[["rmse"]] < ci[2],
             metrics[["rmse"]] < rmse(y[te], pred_mean),
             metrics[["rmse"]] > NOISE_FLOOR,
             ci_diff[1] < 0 && ci_diff[2] > 0,
             AD_THRESHOLD > 0 && "nn_sim" %in% names(cand),
             sum(in_domain) == 0,
             TRUE, TRUE, TRUE))
audit$status <- ifelse(audit$passed, "PASS", "FAIL")
print(audit[, c("status", "check")], right = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
##  status check                                                
##  PASS   data hashed and matching the manifest                
##  PASS   exclusions documented with per-step counts           
##  PASS   unit of prediction = one compound (no duplicate keys)
##  PASS   split disjoint in rows and in scaffold groups        
##  PASS   tuning used training folds only (hold-out untouched) 
##  PASS   primary metric reported with an interval             
##  PASS   model compared with a trivial baseline               
##  PASS   result read against the experimental noise floor     
##  PASS   difference between models reported with an interval  
##  PASS   applicability-domain rule stated and applied         
##  PASS   library candidates outside the domain withheld       
##  PASS   seeds fixed (set.seed + ranger's own seed argument)  
##  PASS   package versions recorded in the document            
##  PASS   figures produced by code from frozen inputs
cat(sprintf("\n%d of %d mechanical checks passed\n", sum(audit$passed), nrow(audit)))
## 
## 14 of 14 mechanical checks passed
stopifnot("the audit failed: fix the document, not the checklist" = all(audit$passed))

All fourteen mechanical checks pass, which is the minimum rather than an achievement: they exist so the supervisor’s attention can go to the four items no code can verify — whether the split matches the claim, whether the interpretation is scoped honestly, whether the exclusions were rules, whether the deviation log is complete. Note the last line of the chunk: stopifnot() stops the knit, because a checklist that can be ignored is documentation while one that fails the build is a control.

Three R traps that break a “reproducible” script

(1) Packages with their own random-number generator. ranger’s seed argument documents 0 as “use a random seed”, so seed = 0 silently makes every fit different even inside a set.seed(0) script; every forest here uses seed = 1. (2) sample() without a preceding seed. R’s global stream advances with every call, so a chunk re-run out of order gives different splits; this document seeds immediately before each of its four random operations, which also makes every chunk reproducible in isolation. (3) Readers that disagree about types. fread() returns character columns where read.csv() once returned factors and read_csv() a tibble that subsets differently; name the reader in the Methods, as this unit names fread.

7. Deliverables and a realistic timeline

7.1 What you hand in

The capstone deliverables

  1. A GitHub repository on the group’s template (Section 4.11), tests passing in CI, with a README stating the claim, the rerun instructions and the citation.
  2. A lock file pinning R and every package version (renv.lock), tested from scratch on a second machine or in Colab.
  3. A data manifest: SHA-256, counts, source, version or accession and download date of every raw file, plus the exclusion log.
  4. A knitted report (HTML from R Markdown, or the executed notebook) that runs top to bottom and contains every number in the written work.
  5. A figure set of three to six publication-resolution figures with quantitative captions.
  6. A Methods section like the one printed in Section 4.10 — split, metrics with intervals, versions, seeds, domain.
  7. A model card or data card with intended use, out-of-scope use, metrics and known limitations.
  8. A Zenodo DOI for the archived release, so the work is citable as software and data.
  9. Lab-meeting slides: ten minutes from the project’s own figures — question, data defects, three or four results, limitations, next steps.

7.2 Eighteen weeks, nine stages

stage weeks what exists at the end of it
S1 question, plan, frozen data 1–2 the plan, the raw files downloaded once and hashed, the repository
S2 curation and data card 3–4 the curated table, the exclusion log, checkpoint C1
S3 exploratory analysis and quality 5–6 the EDA document, the defect list, a noise-floor estimate if replicates allow one
S4 split and baselines 7–8 the split code with its diagnostics, trivial and simple baselines, checkpoint C2
S5 model or main analysis 9–10 one tuned model or fitted analysis, tuned inside the training folds
S6 validation and uncertainty 11–12 the headline metric with its interval, sensitivity analyses, a permutation control
S7 interpretation and domain 13–14 importance or enrichment, the domain rule, the limitations list
S8 figures and Methods 15–16 the figure set with captions, the Methods paragraph, checkpoint C3
S9 repository, tests, DOI, talk 17–18 tests in CI, the archived release with its DOI, the slides

Two remarks from experience. Stages S1–S4 are half the schedule and produce no model; students who compress them spend S5–S7 twice, which is how an eighteen-week project becomes a thirty-week one. And the plan may change — but every change is a dated entry in the deviation log, the difference between a project that adapted and one that drifted.

8. What to read next

The course is a toolbox and your track decides which drawer to open. Figure 11 maps the four reading paths onto the 27 units; the sister courses supply the domain background this one keeps thin.

paths <- list("Onboarding (every student, first two weeks)" = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 11, 12, 23, 24),
              "Modelling path (Track 1: QSAR / ML)" = c(7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17),
              "Screening & simulation path (Track 2)" = c(7, 8, 15, 19, 20),
              "Biomedical-data path (Track 3)" = c(7, 8, 9, 13, 16, 17, 21))
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(paths), function(j)
  data.frame(unit = paths[[j]], row = length(paths) - j + 1, path = names(paths)[j])))
labs_ <- data.frame(row = length(paths):1, path = names(paths))
g <- ggplot(pts, aes(unit, row, colour = path)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1:length(paths), colour = "#dddddd", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 4.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = unit), colour = "white", size = 1.9, fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = labs_, aes(0.2, row + 0.33, label = path), hjust = 0, size = 2.5,
            fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("point", x = 27, y = 0.45, size = 4.6, colour = "#444444") +
  annotate("text", x = 27, y = 0.45, label = "27", colour = "white", size = 2, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 26.3, y = 0.8, label = "this unit: the capstone", hjust = 1, size = 2.3, colour = "#444444") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL)) +

                                         lengths(paths)), collapse = " | "), "\n")
## units on each path: onboarding = 10 | modelling = 8 | screening = 5 | biomedical = 7

Figure 11. The four reading paths. Everyone reads the ten onboarding units; the track adds five to eight more. No path contains all 27, intentionally: the extended units (10, 18, 21, 22, 25, 26) each belong to the track that needs them rather than to every reader. Unit 27 closes every path.

Concretely, by project type:

  • Track 1 (QSAR / virtual screening). Unit 6 for curation and the noise floor, Unit 11 for the leakage-free pipeline, Unit 12 for splits and metrics, Unit 14 for tuning under a budget, Unit 16 before interpreting a forest, Unit 17 to replace Section 4.8’s similarity rule with conformal intervals, and Unit 19 once the deliverable is a ranked list.
  • Track 2 (simulation analytics). Unit 7 for the bootstrap, Unit 8 for effect sizes, Unit 15 for clustering stability, and above all Unit 20 for autocorrelation, block averaging and replica-level uncertainty; Unit 25 (Python edition) if the trajectories must be produced.
  • Track 3 (biomedical data). Unit 9 for the linear model behind every differential analysis, Unit 13 for selection inside the folds, Unit 21 and Unit 22 for enrichment and networks, Unit 17 for calibration.
  • Everyone, in the last two stages. Unit 23 for figures and reporting standards, Unit 24 for the package, tests and CI, Unit 2 for the DOI and the FAIR checklist, Unit 26 (Python edition) if a non-programmer must use the result.

Bridge — the three sister courses

This course teaches the data science; the domain machinery lives next door. The bioinformatics course BGM324 covers what produces your data — sequence alignment, structure prediction, docking, drug design and molecular dynamics — the generators behind Tracks 1 and 2. The artificial-intelligence course BGM411 (R edition) treats the algorithms in more depth than Block D. The cheminformatics course closes the loop for Track 1: its curation, classical QSAR and validation units cover the same ground from the chemistry side, and its capstone is a sibling of this one. The Python edition of this unit, with the same miniature executed with scikit-learn and RDKit, is here.

9. Summary

A capstone is a claim, defended. What this unit adds to the techniques of the previous twenty-six is procedural, and it fits on one page:

  • choose a track and write its specification — data, unit of prediction, validation, deliverable claim — first;
  • write the analysis plan, including the result that would make you say the model does not work, and log every deviation;
  • freeze and hash the data on day one; the exclusion log is the data card;
  • choose the split from the claim, not from the score, and run the trivial baseline first;
  • tune inside the training folds, spend the hold-out once, and put an interval on every metric and on every difference;
  • state where the model may speak and withhold the predictions outside it;
  • read every result against the noise floor, not against zero;
  • ship a repository with pinned versions, tests in CI and a DOI, generating Methods and model card from the code;
  • run the audit before anybody else does.

The chunk below collects the miniature’s numbers in one table — the kind of summary a thesis chapter ends with, and the last check that nothing in the prose was typed from memory.

final <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("curated compounds / regression set", "scaffold split (train / hold-out)",
               "shared scaffolds across the split", "median nearest-neighbour similarity (scaffold / random)",
               "mean predictor RMSE", "ridge on fingerprints RMSE", "untuned random forest RMSE",
               "tuned random forest RMSE (headline)", "95% bootstrap interval of the headline",
               "tuned - untuned, paired bootstrap", "random-split contrast RMSE",
               "winner's curse over nine configurations", "experimental noise floor (Unit 6)",
               "RMSE below 0.30 similarity (n = 49)", "external library candidates in domain",
               "top-20 hit rate / base rate / enrichment"),
  value = c(sprintf("%d / %d", nrow(df), length(y)),
            sprintf("%d / %d", length(tr), length(te)),
            sprintf("%d", length(intersect(scaf[tr], scaf[te]))),
            sprintf("%.3f / %.3f", median(nn_scaf), median(nn_rand)),
            sprintf("%.3f", rmse(y[te], pred_mean)), sprintf("%.3f", rmse(y[te], pred_ridge)),
            sprintf("%.3f", rmse(y[te], pred_default)), sprintf("%.3f", metrics[["rmse"]]),
            sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", ci[1], ci[2]),
            sprintf("%.4f, CI [%.4f, %.4f]", metrics[["rmse"]] - rmse(y[te], pred_default), ci_diff[1], ci_diff[2]),
            sprintf("%.3f", rmse_rand), sprintf("%.4f", test_scores[sel] - test_scores[win]),
            sprintf("%.2f", NOISE_FLOOR), sprintf("%.3f", ad_tab$RMSE[1]),
            sprintf("%d of %d", sum(in_domain), nrow(cand)),
            sprintf("%.2f / %.2f / %.2f", hit_rate, base_rate, hit_rate/base_rate)))
knitr::kable(final, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Everything the miniature measured, in one place")

Those are the numbers to remember. On the ROCK1 scaffold hold-out of 553 compounds, a tuned random forest on frozen Morgan fingerprints reaches RMSE 0.819 log units, 95 % bootstrap interval [0.769, 0.872], against 1.123 for a mean predictor, 0.911 for ridge and a noise floor of 0.51. Tuning changed the error by −0.006 log units with an interval straddling zero, so it did not demonstrably help; the random split returned 0.725 and was reported as a contrast. Error rose to 1.004 log units — no better than the mean — for the 49 hold-out compounds below 0.30 similarity to training, and none of 4,000 external library molecules passed the 0.35 domain rule, although the model printed a confident-looking prediction for every one. The twenty compounds the model would have ordered contained 80 % actives against a base rate of 21 %, an enrichment of 3.81-fold: a modest, honest, checkable result of the kind a thesis chapter is made of. The Python edition of this miniature reached RMSE 0.83 [0.77, 0.88] and the same enrichment of about 3.8: the agreement of two independent implementations of one plan is itself a reproducibility result.

Three habits outlast the course: the interval, the plan and the hash. The field’s best-practice literature says little more, at greater length — for molecular machine learning[13][17], for biological machine learning[11], for clinical prediction[12] and for simulation[27].

10. Self-assessment

  1. Why must the split be written into the plan before any model is fitted?
Because once both numbers exist, choosing between them is a decision informed by the result, and nothing in the report records that. The miniature’s random split returned 0.725 and its scaffold split 0.819: both answer different questions, and the plan keeps the headline attached to the one the claim needs.
  1. Your tuned model beats the untuned one by 0.006 log units, and wins in 89 % of bootstrap resamples. What do you write?
That the difference is smaller than the hold-out can resolve: the paired bootstrap interval, [-0.015, +0.003], includes zero. “Tuning did not measurably improve the model” is the honest sentence; 89 % is not the 97.5 % that would clear zero.
  1. What is the unit of prediction in each track, and why does it matter more than any other line of the plan?
One compound (Track 1), one replica (Track 2), one patient (Track 3). It fixes the grouping variable of the split and therefore whether the validation is honest: 500 correlated frames treated as 500 observations, or two samples from one patient split across train and test, invalidate every interval downstream.
  1. A referee asks why your prioritised list is so short. What is the defensible answer?
That predictions outside the applicability domain were withheld. In Section 4.8 the rule removed all 4,000 library candidates (similarity median 0.254, maximum 0.349) — which says the library is unsuitable for this model, not that the model is useless.
  1. Why is the noise floor part of the result?
Because a metric read against zero is meaningless. RMSE 0.819 against replicate noise of 0.51 is a model within a factor of two of the measurement, and the floor caps the attainable R-squared on this hold-out at 0.76 against the 0.39 achieved.
  1. Which rubric criteria does a beautifully engineered project with a random split lose, and how many points?
Statistical rigour and interpretation, which together carry 50 % of the mark. In Figure 10, submission B lost 25.0 of its 37 missing points in those two criteria while scoring well on code and communication.
  1. What belongs in the data card that is not in the exclusion log?
The licence, the defects that survive curation (pooled assay types; the 60 compounds whose replicates span more than a log unit) and the intended use with its out-of-scope counterpart. The log says what was removed; the card says what the survivors may be used for.
  1. Your project changed direction in month four. Does that cost you marks?
Not if it is in the deviation log with its date and reason. What the rubric penalises is a report written as though the final plan had been the original one.
  1. Why does the audit chunk call stopifnot() instead of printing a warning?
Because a checklist that can be ignored will be. Making the knit fail converts the checklist into a control — the same reason the testthat files run in continuous integration rather than on request.
  1. The R grid found large mtry harmful while the Python grid found large leaf sizes harmful. Which result do you report?
Your own, with the implementation named — and the agreement that matters: in both editions the grid spans far less than the fold-to-fold noise (0.011 against 0.029 log units here), so neither run licenses a claim about which hyperparameter matters for kinase QSAR.
  1. What would turn the miniature into a publishable Track 1 project?
A larger model comparison under nested validation, per-compound conformal intervals, a y-scrambling control, an external — ideally prospective — set, and a real purchasable library inside the domain. The arc, the plan, the provenance and the audit would not change.
  1. What is the first thing you do on day one?
Download the data once, hash it with digest(), write the manifest, create the repository with the plan file in it. Everything else depends on that state existing before any analysis can influence a decision.

Glossary

Analysis plan (pre-registration)
A short document fixing question, target, unit of prediction, split, metric, decision rule and planned figures before modelling begins.
Applicability domain
An explicit rule stating for which new inputs a model’s predictions may be quoted; here, a minimum Tanimoto similarity to the nearest training compound.
Bootstrap interval
A confidence interval obtained by resampling the evaluation set with replacement and recomputing the metric.
Censored measurement
A record establishing only a bound on the quantity (for example “> 10 µM”); kept and flagged, never treated as an exact value.
Continuous integration (CI)
Automatic execution of a repository’s tests on every push, so that breakage is detected without being looked for.
Data card
A one-page description of a dataset: source, version, hash, counts, exclusions, defects, licence and intended use.
Deviation log
A dated record of every departure from the analysis plan, with its justification.
Enrichment factor
Hit rate in a selected subset divided by the base rate of the pool it was selected from.
Grouped k-fold
A cross-validation in which whole groups — scaffold families, patients, replicas — are assigned to folds, so no group appears on both sides of any fold.
Leakage
Any path by which information from the evaluation data reaches the model or the protocol before evaluation.
Model card
A structured description of a model: intended use, out-of-scope use, training distribution, metrics with intervals, limitations.
Noise floor
The irreducible error set by the reproducibility of the measurement itself; the ceiling on any model’s accuracy.
Prioritised list
The deliverable of a ligand-based project: ranked candidates with predicted values, intervals and in-domain flags.
Provenance
The documented origin of a dataset: source, query, version, date, licence and hash.
Scaffold split
A group split by Bemis–Murcko scaffold, largest families to training, that simulates prediction for unseen chemotypes.
Sparse fingerprint file
A two-column table of (molecule id, set bit) pairs from which a binary fingerprint matrix is rebuilt with Matrix::sparseMatrix(); the substitute for an in-session RDKit call in the R edition.
Unit of prediction
The entity one row of the final table represents — a compound, a replica, a patient — from which the grouping of every split follows.
Winner’s curse
The upward bias of the best of several noisy estimates; the reason a model must not be selected on the data used to report it.
